question: The lecturer points out that one particular downturn is referred to by two different names in the discussion — one name draws a direct parallel to the 1930s crisis, and the other name highlights that the recession was felt across the whole world. What are those two names?
answer_key: The Great Recession (named as a parallel to the Great Depression) and the Global Financial Crisis (because the recession was felt all around the world).
notes: Supporting text (chunk 12): 'This episode here is is called the Great Recession, as a parallel for the Great Depression... And it's also known as the Global Financial Crisis, because this was a recession all around the world.' Anti-leakage: question paraphrases without naming the two terms.

question: The lecture walks through a real payroll data release that surprised the stock market. Before the number came out, what job-growth figure had forecasters been expecting, and what was the actual number that ended up beating that forecast so dramatically?
answer_key: Forecasters expected non-farm job growth of about 190,000; the actual reported figure came in at over 500,000 jobs added.
notes: chunk 29 supports the expected figure: 'people expected ... the payroll to increase ... by about 190,000 workers.' chunk 30 supports the actual figure: 'the actual change in the payroll was not 190k. It was over a 500,000k.' Removing either chunk leaves the surprise/comparison incomplete.

question: In the opening lecture for MIT's 14.02 Principles of Macroeconomics — the one where the professor says he won't actually be teaching that day and instead just explains what macro is about and shows recent charts on inflation, wages, and the stock market — what are the main threads the professor uses to introduce the course and its goals?
answer_key: He first distinguishes macro (aggregate, whole-economy phenomena) from micro (individual households/firms) using a physics-style analogy; states the course's goal is not to train math-heavy researchers but to let students critically read publications like the IMF's World Economic Outlook or the Wall Street Journal; then uses a string of real post-COVID events — inflation, wage growth, historically low unemployment, central bank rate hikes, equity market swings, and China's reopening — to preview the kinds of interconnected macro relationships the course's simple models will explain.
reference_points: 区分宏观(整体经济现象:通胀、失业、汇率)与微观(单个家庭/企业)，用物理学中研究大物体与小粒子方法不同做类比
课程目标不是培养数学化的宏观研究者,而是让学生能批判性地读懂IMF《世界经济展望》、华尔街日报等出版物
用工资增长与通胀高度相关的图表说明当下的宏观议题:失业率处于历史低位,同时通胀达到80年代以来最高水平
用最新的非农就业数据发布(预期19万,实际超50万)现场演示股市为何应声下跌——市场预期美联储将因此加息
用中国零疫情政策导致经济放缓、以及解封后预期反弹对拉美等大宗商品出口国的外溢效应作为全球案例
提到大多数专业预测者认为今年美国衰退概率约65%,原因是美联储为对抗通胀持续加息
notes: 消歧锚点:课程编号'MIT 14.02 Principles of Macroeconomics'+'开篇课/第一课'+'教授说当天不上课只讲macro是什么'这一具体细节，与其他视频区分。reference_points取自该视频L2摘要及正文。

question: Kun looks at one specific skills repository on GitHub that has an enormous star count (177,000+) and decides to actually benchmark one of its skills instead of just trusting the star count. What did his benchmark find about token usage and output quality, and whose work does he point out the skill wasn't actually written by?
answer_key: The benchmark showed that using that skill made the agent use about 5% more tokens while producing worse results; Kun also notes the skill wasn't actually written by André (Andrej) Karpathy himself, despite being commonly associated with his name.
notes: Supporting text (chunk 30): 'Look at this repo here called Android Skills, which has 177,000 GitHub stars... I actually evaluated a skill in this repo with Program Bench... the agent will use 5% more tokens while making the results worse. And if you look closely, this skill is not even written by André Karpathy himself.' ('Android Skills' is the manifest's literal transcription, likely a mishearing of an Anthropic/Claude-skills-type repo name; question avoids repeating this ambiguous name.)

question: Kun ran his own benchmark comparing different ways of letting an agent access GitHub. According to that benchmark, roughly how many times more expensive (in tokens) and how much slower is the GitHub MCP server versus just calling the CLI directly, and which one tool in the same comparison came out on top for both spending the least and succeeding the most?
answer_key: The GitHub MCP server costs roughly three times more tokens and more than double the latency compared to the CLI for equivalent tasks. His own tool, Axi, tops that same comparison by being the cheapest option while also succeeding the most often.
notes: chunk 35 supports the GitHub MCP vs CLI comparison: '...using GitHub, MCP server will cost you to spend three times more on token cost, and more than double the latency compared to using the CLI.' chunk 36 supports Axi winning: '...this thing called axi, which has the lowest cost but highest success rate.' Removing either chunk leaves the comparison or the winner unknown. Anti-leakage: question rewords 'lowest cost but highest success rate' as 'cheapest option while also succeeding the most often'.

question: In the walkthrough by a former principal engineer (who worked at Meta, Microsoft, and Atlassian) that frames his whole agent-engineering setup around a ship-and-crew metaphor — captain, crewmates, and eventually a first mate — what are the main stages he goes through to build up this workflow?
answer_key: He starts by 'building the ship' (a fully keyboard-driven terminal setup with WezTerm, tmux, and Neovim), then 'recruits crewmates' by onboarding agents through global and project-level memory files plus modular skills, then shows working with a single crewmate (voice input, planning via his own tool 'Lavish', and an automated review/PR pipeline called 'No Mistakes'), then scales up to multiple crewmates in parallel using git worktrees, and finally recruits a 'first mate' — an orchestration agent that manages the whole crew so the captain can focus on higher-level direction.
reference_points: 整体用'船长-船员'比喻组织全文:组装船(终端环境WezTerm+tmux+Neovim)->招募并培训船员(记忆文件+技能)->与单个船员协作->同时管理多个船员->招募大副(first mate)统筹全部
偏好全键盘、终端为中心的工作流,理由是保持心流不被鼠标打断、且能在Mac/Windows/Linux及手机上保持完全一致的体验(通过tmux持久会话)
用全局记忆文件(精简,记录个人偏好如不给AI预估开发成本过高的权重)+项目级记忆文件(积累项目专属经验)来培训agent,再把只在特定场景需要的内容迁移进'技能(skills)'以节省token(渐进式披露)
提醒不要盲目安装网络上高星标的技能,并用自己的基准测试证明某个177k+star的技能实际上会让agent多耗5%的token且效果更差
用自建工具Lavish把纯文字的方案讨论变成可视化、可直接点选反馈的HTML原型,减少'读大段文字'的负担
完成后不逐行review diff,而是丢给自建的No Mistakes流水线(对抗式审查、端到端测试、文档更新、发PR并持续跟到合并),把自己定位成'工程经理'而非代码审查者
用Good Night Have Fun做长时间无人值守的自主任务,再用git worktree(通过自建的Treehouse简化)+First Mate来同时编排多个并行的agent会话
notes: 消歧锚点:'former principal engineer'背景(Meta/Microsoft/Atlassian)+'船长-船员'比喻+具体自建工具名(Lavish/No Mistakes/Good Night Have Fun/First Mate)。reference_points取自该视频L2摘要及正文。

question: In the section on weighted load-balancing algorithms, the lecture gives a concrete example of three servers with different amounts of RAM to show how weights get assigned. What RAM values are given for the first, second, and third servers in that example?
answer_key: 16 GB for the first server, 32 GB for the second, and 64 GB for the third — with the load balancer sending proportionally more traffic to the servers with more RAM/performance.
notes: Supporting text (chunk 32): 'if the first server has 16 gigs of RAM, the second one has 32, and the third one has 64... based on the server RAM and other metrics, they are assigned two weights.'

question: The lecture explains why certain kinds of APIs should be built on one particular transport-layer protocol rather than the other. Which protocol does it recommend for something like a payments or banking API, and what exact guarantee does the faster alternative give up in order to be lighter-weight?
answer_key: TCP is recommended for payment/banking/authentication-type APIs, because it guarantees ordered, reliable delivery (resending lost or out-of-order packets after a three-way handshake). The faster alternative, UDP, gives up the delivery guarantee entirely — if a packet is lost, UDP simply does not resend it.
notes: chunk 90 supports TCP for payments: 'That's why APIs that involve payments, authentication, or user data always use TCP.' chunk 91 supports what UDP gives up: '...there is no delivery guarantee. There is also no handshake...' Removing either chunk leaves the comparison incomplete. Per BATCH_INSTRUCTIONS special rule for this video: this is a real-chunk detail/multi_evidence question, unrelated to the broken L2 (CSRF/XSS section summary); no summary question was written for this video (see final report).

question: The lecture describes an attempt to replicate empirical papers that had been published in a journal on money, credit, and banking in the early 1980s. Of the papers examined in depth, how many could be reproduced exactly, and what share of the authors of the earlier batch of papers never even got back to the researchers when they asked for the underlying data?
answer_key: Only 2 of the 9 papers examined in depth could be reproduced exactly; about two-thirds of the earlier papers' authors never responded when asked to share their data (even after a mid-1982 policy requiring authors to archive data and code, a quarter of later authors still didn't respond).
notes: Supporting text (chunk 9): '...even among papers accepted after that date however one quarter of the authors failed to respond... a shocking two-thirds of the authors of earlier papers failed to respond... only two of the nine papers analyzed in depth by dewald at all could be reproduced exactly.' Anti-leakage: question rephrases 'failed to respond' as 'never even got back to the researchers'.

question: In David Card's Sveriges Riksbank (Nobel) Prize lecture — the one that traces the rise of design-based empirical methods through his own studies of the Mariel boatlift and the New Jersey/Pennsylvania minimum-wage comparison — what overall arc does he use to make his case for research design in economics?
answer_key: Card opens with the 1970s-80s 'credibility gap' in applied economics (failed macro models and unreliable econometric estimates), then traces the rise of design-based/natural-experiment methods through his own landmark studies, lays out three strengths of research designs (transparent causality, policy relevance, portability across settings), rebuts three common criticisms of the approach, and closes by noting how his controversial minimum-wage findings eventually helped move employer wage-setting power closer to mainstream acceptance.
reference_points: 开场回顾1970-80年代应用经济学的'可信度危机':宏观模型失灵,Lalonde 1986年论文显示计量方法脱离真实对照组会给出很不可靠、跨度很大的估计
引用Dewald等人的复制研究:《货币信贷与银行学刊》多数已发表实证结果无法复现,很多作者拒绝提供数据
以自己的两项标志性研究为例说明'研究设计'路径的兴起:1990年马列尔海运(Mariel boatlift)移民劳动力市场研究、与Alan Krueger合作的新泽西/宾夕法尼亚最低工资对比研究
总结研究设计的三大优势:把因果关系讲清楚(transparent causality)、便于非专业人士理解且直接对政策相关、可移植到不同情境重复验证
回应三类常见批评(结论过于情境特定、模型过于简化、无法外推到样本之外的场景),并逐一说明这些批评被夸大或可通过后续研究弥补
指出尽管当年遭到加里·贝克尔、詹姆斯·布坎南等经济学家猛烈批评,他的最低工资研究最终推动了'雇主具有工资设定权'这一观点逐渐进入主流劳动经济学
结尾感谢导师与合作者,并把演讲献给三位已故的同事:Alan Krueger、John DiNardo和Bob LaLonde
notes: 消歧锚点:'David Card'+'Sveriges Riksbank Prize'(诺贝尔经济学奖)+具体研究'Mariel boatlift'与'New Jersey/Pennsylvania minimum wage'研究,与库内其他经济学视频区分。reference_points取自该视频L2摘要及正文。
